strengths: The paper addresses an important practical problem: improving specialized reasoning or task performance of frozen LLMs without full fine-tuning. A plug-and-play module that can be trained cheaply and reused with larger frozen backbones would be useful if robust.

The core mechanism is simple and appealing: train a smaller reasoning policy with rule-based rewards, then add its logits to the frozen backbone at inference. This gives the method a clean modular interface and makes composition of task-specialized modules natural.

The empirical section is reasonably broad. The paper evaluates mathematical reasoning, translation, transfer to larger backbones, module composition, memory use, and additional VLM experiments. The gains for Llama3.2 math and the transfer/composition demonstrations are promising.

The work is mostly clearly presented. The method, prompts, hyperparameters, and reward definitions are described in enough detail to make the approach understandable, and the qualitative examples help explain the intended behavior of the reasoning module.

The computational-efficiency argument is credible on the training side: updating only a small reasoning module while freezing the backbone should reduce activation and optimizer memory relative to full fine-tuning and often LoRA.
weaknesses: The theoretical framing is overstated. Equation (4) assumes a trajectory reward can be represented as a sum of log-probabilities from a policy, but log-probabilities are normalized, length-dependent, and nonpositive up to constants. The paper cites reward-equivalence intuition, but does not carefully handle normalization constants, sequence-length effects, or the conditions under which this representation yields valid token-level guidance.

The claim of architecture-agnostic or universal transfer is stronger than the evidence supports. Logit addition requires compatible vocabularies/tokenizers and aligned token semantics; the experiments mostly transfer within model families. The paper should qualify the claim or explain how UniR works across genuinely different tokenizers and output spaces.

The empirical improvements are meaningful but mixed. UniR clearly helps over the base model and naive logit summation, but for Qwen math it underperforms full GRPO and slightly underperforms GRPO-LoRA on average, while translation gains over full GRPO are small. This supports usefulness, but not the strongest version of the superiority claims.

The baselines are not fully satisfying. Stronger comparisons to inference-time guidance, reward-model-guided decoding, product-of-experts/logit ensembling, learned reranking, and better-tuned LoRA/GRPO variants would help isolate whether UniR’s advantage comes from the proposed decomposition rather than from baseline tuning choices.

Inference-time cost is underanalyzed. The method requires an additional model forward pass during decoding, but the paper mainly reports training memory. Latency, throughput, total token cost, and the quality-cost tradeoff versus sampling/reranking or fine-tuning are important for assessing practical significance.

Reproducibility is decent but incomplete. Prompts and hyperparameters are included, and the paper claims code release, but the code URL appears missing in the abstract. More details on hardware, wall-clock training time, random seeds, variance across runs, and exact evaluation scripts would make the results easier to verify.

The limitations discussion is honest but too brief on safety and misuse. Dynamically guiding frozen LLMs with external modules could affect reliability, controllability, and harmful-content behavior; the paper does not evaluate whether UniR preserves safety alignment or whether composed modules can produce unintended interactions.
